- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.

Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. ## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups

# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Lessons from the 2026-09-27 review wave (Supertraining Ch2-3, Issurin Ch3, Bondarchuk, Evans, Old Bull)

- **Invented Examples are the most common failure.** 34 of 36 Supertraining Ch2-3a Examples were unlabelled inventions. Use the source's own example where it gives one; otherwise start the Example with "Inference:".
- **"Verified against the page image" means you opened the image.** Four Issurin Ch3 entries claimed it for figures they had misread (Fig 3.7 inverted, a Table 3.7 row swapped). Sparse slides are not "bare diagrams" until you have looked.
- **Name the population and method the source gives.** Bondarchuk's data are 7,000+ native and foreign athletes, questionnaires, r >= 0.349, steroid-free; entries that said "Soviet athletes" were wrong everywhere.
- **Check what a cited paper actually says.** Issurin 2016's critique targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, not Issurin's A-T-R; Herzog & Leonard 2000 shows force enhancement, against the book's sentence. When the book misreports a study, record both.
- **No review history in entries.** "Prior version", "corrected from a NO-GO finding" and similar belong in `staging/fixes_*_applied.md`, never in the entry body.
- **Fix logs must match the files.** One fixer log claimed fixes that were not made. Fixers run their own grep checks and paste the output.
- **Section headers use the vault form** `**What it is** —` (with the em dash). Do not add suffixes such as ": mandatory". Em dashes are banned only in titles and body text. Never wrap a `[[wikilink]]` across lines.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.
- **OCR confidence scores miss the worst errors** (checked 2026-09-27). Zatsiorsky 2e: the OCR interleaves the two columns and the sidebars line by line, so its text is not readable prose; use it only to find content, and read and quote from the page image. *CFTS*: single-column prose that mostly reads in order, but upside-down lines come out as gibberish, some lines are dropped, and figures are scrambled, all at "0 low-confidence pages". For any OCR source, quote only after checking the page image, and read every figure and table from the image.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

## Baylor context

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

## Scope and output

- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.
- Final reply: entries by kind and by confidence; chapters or units done and pending with page ranges; reciprocal-link suggestions; unclear or contradictory spots in the source; anything you could not read.

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally reports a league-wide study, "under review" at the time of the talk, using public MLB data (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Window:** 2004 to 2014, chosen so that players who had surgery in 2014 had time to return (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Counts:** about 200 surgeries, and on average 180 days of MLB-calendar time missed (z_6M5r7031A [12:14]). About half the players were starters and half relievers, with a small proportion of closers (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Total:** adjusted to 2017 levels, "half a billion dollars" of salary lost over the period to rehab alone (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Excluded:** medical, travel and rehab costs; downtime before the surgery; lost team wins; trade value; and every minor league player (z_6M5r7031A [12:44] to [13:44]). He speculates the full cost might be 1 billion or 1.5 billion and says "I don't know" (z_6M5r7031A [13:44]).
- **Per player:** medical cost of about $50,000, which he calls conservative (z_6M5r7031A [11:13]). (Untested: bare assertion, no method given.)
- **Salary per WAR:** it "balloons" after surgery and does not return to the pre-surgery level until 3 years after the pitcher returns (z_6M5r7031A [10:43]). In Q&A he calls the salary-over-WAR calculation "relatively back of the envelope" and not adjusted (z_6M5r7031A [28:27]). (Untested: back-of-envelope, unadjusted.)

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism; this is an accounting of public salary data. Inference: it counts only direct salary during rehab, which is why the number is a floor on the speaker's own account.

**When to apply** — As an example of costing an injury type from public records by counting time missed and attaching a value. Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: a Baylor version would count games and practices missed by injury type and position group with Athletic Medicine, with no salary figure.

**When NOT to apply** — The study was under review, not published, at the time. Baylor athletes have no player salaries, so dollar figures and dollars per WAR do not transfer to college. The salary-per-WAR calculation is unadjusted and the speaker's own words are "back of the envelope." The 180-day figure is MLB calendar time. It is professional baseball pitchers only, and it counts surgeries, not all injuries.

**Example** — The speaker's own: about 200 surgeries over 2004 to 2014 and 180 MLB-calendar days missed on average, summing to half a billion 2017 dollars (z_6M5r7031A [12:14] to [12:44]).

The claim that a low-physical, high-psychological player succeeds at first-round-star rates compares failure rates, not careers. Do not use as a recruiting rule: it is an NFL draft result. Inference: the speakers present their own test, so the talk is not an independent evaluation of it.

# Validate an Assessment Before Using It: Score Early, Rate Later, Correlate

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Ken yuso"; the speaker thanks co-authors "Charles sheram" and Harold Goldstein, 40NV3_u9tYY [00:03]) describes a three-step validation of the NFL's one-hour psychological test. His background: industrial and organizational psychologists, "heavy litigation, employment discrimination" work, where "you have to demonstrate that what you're measuring actually is connected to some meaningful outcome" (40NV3_u9tYY [08:21], [08:52]). Design as reported:
- **Predictor:** the assessment taken at the combine before any NFL playing time; 1,500 player scores over three years, about 330 combine participants a year plus a "Super Regional" (40NV3_u9tYY [08:52]).
- **Criteria:** team coaches' ratings on about 24 dimensions after the player had been on the team at least a year, with about 70% participation across all 32 teams per year (40NV3_u9tYY [09:22], [09:54]); also on-field metrics (penalties per play, yards per penalty) and injuries (40NV3_u9tYY [16:35], [17:37]).
- **Sample:** about 500 players with performance data (40NV3_u9tYY [09:54]).
- **Results (decimal points are garbled in the captions: "0 28", "about3", "a0 29", "about 35"):** about 0.28 (the caption does not say which measure), about 0.3 for the cognitive composite, about 0.29 for the personality composite, about 0.35 combined (40NV3_u9tYY [10:24], [10:56], [11:26], [15:33]). The speaker calls the correlations "uncorrected", "extremely conservative" and good for behavioral science (40NV3_u9tYY [10:24]).
The speaker adds "no test as a crystal ball" and that the test is meant as an addition to physical and skills measures (40NV3_u9tYY [11:57], [10:24]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is the standard predictive validity logic: measure first, then check against what happens later (40NV3_u9tYY [09:54]: "a classic validation study"). The mechanism by which a trait score would produce coach ratings is not given. Inference: the key protection is that the predictor is collected before the outcome exists, which the speaker describes, though the talk does not say whether coaches saw the test results (see the limits below).

**When to apply** — When deciding whether to add or keep a test. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." Eric's baseline (explicit, `2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`): "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data." Inference: a before-and-after check of a candidate Baylor measure against a later outcome (a coach rating, an availability record) is a cheap way to meet that rule, with the outcome chosen first.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is supported, not proven: the speakers report the method and correlations, but give no confidence intervals, no subgroup sizes and no position splits. The main criterion is coach opinion, not performance. The talk does not say whether coaches saw the test scores before rating (40NV3_u9tYY [09:22], per the summary's limits). The speakers run the assessment, so this is not an independent evaluation, and co-author Harold Goldstein was absent (40NV3_u9tYY [00:03]). Participation was "about 70%" (40NV3_u9tYY [09:22]), so non-response is possible, and Inference: the sample is combine participants rated after at least a year with a team, so early-career players. Correlations near 0.3 explain about 9% of variance (Inference: arithmetic on r squared), so use them for broad sorting, not individual calls.

**Example** — The speakers' own: the test scores taken at the combine against ratings given a year or more later for "learn the game readily", mental errors, decisions under stress, leadership, work ethic and similar dimensions (40NV3_u9tYY [10:56], [11:26]).

**Related** — [[claim--score-bands-map-to-coach-rating-odds]], [[claim--decisions-under-stress-needs-ability-plus-stress-tolerance]], [[principle--add-standardized-psychological-data-as-increment-not-substitute]]; existing library: [[heuristic--fix-protocol-before-trusting-a-noisy-metric]] (Old Bull), and the research brief [[farrell-2024-beyond-the-box-score-using-psychological-metrics-to-forecast-nba-success]].

confidence: untested

# Cluster Players on Physical and Psychological Scores Together to Find Types, Not Single Scores

**What it is** — The second speaker (caption spelling "Charles sheram") argues that the psychological characteristics had been studied "really in isolation", so the next step is the multivariate profile: "different types of players who have different constellations" and how each relates to "derailment or risk factors" (40NV3_u9tYY [19:44], [20:14]). Method: cluster analysis and mixture models, borrowed from market research (profiling customers by behavior and attitude), applied to 2014 to 2016 data (40NV3_u9tYY [21:16], [21:46], [22:16]). Inputs: coach-rated physical talent plus the psychological scores, shown as z-scores (40NV3_u9tYY [22:16], [22:47]). Output: nine profiles, for example:
- Cluster 7: above average on physical and on the psychological scores, "the whole package" (40NV3_u9tYY [22:47]).
- Cluster 9: above average psychologically, less physically talented (40NV3_u9tYY [22:47]).

# Defensive Three-Point Percentage Looks Like a Coin Flip, Yet Defenders Affect Shots: "Defending the Three Means Avoiding It"

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now") says defensive three-point percentage, at team or individual level, is "not really a thing", a point he describes as one note the writers of Nylon Calculus have hit many times and which he endorses (BJkCqf6Fj2w [15:48], [16:18]), because what happens once the shot leaves the offensive player's hands is "out of the defense's hands". Support: a graph by another writer (caption spelling "Hest Becker") indicating that individual defensive three-point percentage "looks a lot like a coin flip would look" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [16:18]). He then qualifies it: he is "not saying that it is just luck", only that it looks like it would if it were (BJkCqf6Fj2w [16:48]). Where defenders do affect a shot:
- Distance: a shooter four feet from the defender on a catch-and-shoot shoots about 34%, at ten feet about 40% (BJkCqf6Fj2w [16:48], [17:18]).
- Fouls: fouling a jump shooter "turns a 35% shot into a 75 or 80% shot" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [17:18]).
- Late shot clock and end-of-game situations show low three-point percentages "even controlling for all other factors", but he says that style of defense is not available in regular play, because a defender must also stop the drive (BJkCqf6Fj2w [17:18], [17:48]).
His conclusion: a catch-and-shoot three below roughly 34% is usually not taken, and "even a 34% three is a 51% effective shot", so "defending the three means avoiding the three entirely" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [17:48], [18:19]). He uses baseball's batting average on balls in play (BABIP) as the analogy, noting that in baseball the "no control" idea was later "relaxed a fair amount" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [15:18], [15:48]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives a partial mechanism: the contest affects the shot through distance, fouls and clock context, and most of the defensive effect shows up as shots not taken (BJkCqf6Fj2w [15:18], [18:19]). The coin-flip comparison itself is shown with a graph by another writer and no detail.

**When to apply** — As a caution against using an outcome rate the defense does not control as a skill metric, and as an example of the risk of reading a flat distribution as "luck". Inference: the same caution applies to any Baylor metric whose variation looks random at the individual level, where one should ask what the measure does not capture before using it to judge a person. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2a): "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a)**

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested, not contested: the speaker reconciles the two points himself ("not saying that it is just luck... it looks a lot like it would if it was just luck", BJkCqf6Fj2w [16:48]) and lists real defender effects (distance, fouls, late clock) alongside. The coin-flip evidence is a single graph from another writer with no detail shown, and the 34% and 40% figures have no sample or source stated aloud. The caption "worth 50% less" at 20 feet at the end of the talk is unclear (BJkCqf6Fj2w [19:50]) and should not be relied on. NBA only; a statement about one metric, not about defensive skill in general.

**Example** — The talk's: a 34% three is a 51% effective shot, so a defense cannot make such shots unattractive except by preventing them (BJkCqf6Fj2w [18:19]).

**Related** — [[principle--basketball-possession-has-a-third-outcome-not-shooting]], [[claim--four-drivers-of-rising-three-point-rate]].

# Four Drivers of More Threes: Skill, Permission, Downsizing and Catching the Ball Farther Out

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spellings "Seth part now" and, in the intro, "Seth partau") ends with what he calls "one truth" and then says all of it is "still just a theory" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [18:19], [20:51]). Teams work harder to create threes because a longer jump shot is more valuable than the jump shots already taken. Four factors (BJkCqf6Fj2w [18:50], [19:20], [19:50]):
- **Individual skill development:** players working more on long-distance shooting because the three "is a vital piece to getting playing time" and staying in the league.
- **Permission:** teams encourage and permit players with that skill to step out and shoot.
- **Downsizing:** less time with two traditional big men and more shooters on the floor.
- **Strategy that changes where players catch the ball:** to take a catch-and-shoot three, the ball must be caught outside the arc, so teams changed where players catch it; "worth 50% less" at 20 feet is unclear in the captions (BJkCqf6Fj2w [19:50]).
Evidence for the net effect: perimeter players have long had high three-point rates, but over the last four years power forwards' three-point rate "jumped substantially", most teams play with four shooters and this year more often five (BJkCqf6Fj2w [20:20], [20:51]). His summary: "people are stepping further away from the basket" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [20:51]). In Q&A he adds a limit: there is "probably" a ceiling on how many players have the skill to space the floor (BJkCqf6Fj2w [23:56]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives these as his theory and does not test any one cause. Inference: with four causes named together and no attribution among them, the account cannot say which one mattered most.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when explaining a league-wide strategy shift: ask separately about skill supply, coach permission, roster design and scheme. Inference: Baylor's analogue is any change in practice or testing culture, where individual skill, staff permission, roster mix and process changes may each contribute and should be asked about separately.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the speaker's own theory, with the only data a power-forward rate chart that the captions do not describe. He says everyone should welcome "better theories" to supplant his (BJkCqf6Fj2w [20:51]). He declined to answer a question on how teams measure chains of actions and how advanced they are, saying "I can't talk about it" and then "I'm not going to answer" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [22:25], [22:55]). NBA only, through the 2017 All-Star break (BJkCqf6Fj2w [19:50], captions "through the allstar break of this year").

**Example** — From the talk: power forwards' three-point rate "jumped substantially" over four years while perimeter players' rates were already high (BJkCqf6Fj2w [20:20]).

# The Share of Jump Shots Was 55% in 1999-2000 and 55% Last Year: What Changed Is Distance

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now") tests the complaint that "the NBA has become a jump shooting league" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [04:00]). Reported data, using shot-location data he calls reliable from about 1999-2000:
- Jump shot defined as a shot from outside 10 feet: 55% of shots in 1999-2000 and 55% the previous season (BJkCqf6Fj2w [04:32]).
- Using 15 feet: it started near 42%, peaked at 48%, and is "around 46% now" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [04:32], [05:02]).
- Ten of the last twelve NBA finalists ranked in the top ten in three-point rate that season (BJkCqf6Fj2w [04:00]).
His conclusion: teams have always taken many jump shots, because defenses "protect the paint" and a shot clock forces some shots from farther out; what has risen is how many come from longer distances (BJkCqf6Fj2w [05:02], [05:32]). The same fact is framed two ways ("settling" or "smart strategy", BJkCqf6Fj2w [06:03]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's explanation is that defenses try to prevent layups and dunks, so some shots must be taken from farther away under the shot clock (BJkCqf6Fj2w [05:02], [05:32]). He states the paint-protection point as common knowledge without a citation.

**When to apply** — As a worked example of checking a claim about "more of X" against a time series with a fixed definition. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." Inference: the transferable move is to fix a definition (here "outside 10 feet") and compare the same measure across years before accepting a trend story, as for any Baylor load metric whose definition or threshold changed.

**When NOT to apply** — Supported, not proven: the numbers were spoken from slides the captions do not describe, and the share outside 15 feet is given as three rounded values. The data are NBA, 1999-2000 to "last year" as the speaker says it in March 2017. The definition (10 feet) is the speaker's, and he notes a 15-foot choice changes the series. It shows the share of jump shots did not rise; it says nothing about their efficiency. It is not evidence on any other sport or on college basketball.

**Example** — The speaker's own: 55% in 1999-2000 and 55% last year for shots beyond 10 feet (BJkCqf6Fj2w [04:32]).

# Baseball Analogies Break Where a Basketball Possession Can End With No Shot at All

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now") says many concepts port from baseball to basketball: rate stats over counting stats, efficiency, and treating the possession or shot like a plate appearance (BJkCqf6Fj2w [12:48], [13:18]). Past a certain level of detail, two differences matter (BJkCqf6Fj2w [13:18], [13:48], [14:18]):

Consequence the speaker draws: "a lot of what we would see as having a shot been contested well means that a player doesn't shoot at all" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [15:18]). He cites the corner three as the example: it is one of the most valuable shots yet a small share of attempts, "because you have to do something right beforehand" and the defense is trying to stop it (BJkCqf6Fj2w [14:48]).

The point is limited to basketball and baseball. It does not say baseball metrics are wrong, only that they need adjusting at fine detail.

**Example** — From the talk: a corner three is among the most valuable shots, but few possessions end with one (BJkCqf6Fj2w [14:48]).
